co_wave_boulder_the.blurb: A single long boulder, roughly forty feet across, among the Satellite Boulders in the foothills above Boulder, reached on foot from the Chautauqua side. It holds ten problems and gets harder as you move along it: the left end is mostly V0 and V1 with a traverse that suits warm-ups, while the right end has a V4 and a V5. Landings are mostly flat, though the base sits on a path that other hikers use, so a spotter who watches the trail is handy. A good stop for beginners and intermediates, and an easy add-on to a day of wandering through the neighbouring boulders.
co_wave_boulder_the.approach: Begin at the Chautauqua trailhead. A steeper, busier option climbs by way of the First and Second Flatiron trail; a longer, gentler one follows the Bluebell Baird trail, which reaches the Satellite Boulders after about 1.2 miles.

co_watermark_the.blurb: A small, west-facing crag perched on the south side of Boulder Canyon, above the creek and tucked between Avalon and Vampire Rock. About ten routes, mostly bolted, with a few trad lines mixed in. The grades are friendly: easy fives up through 5.10, with plenty in the middle that make good first outdoor leads. The climbing is on slabs with a handful of roofs and overhangs. Because it faces west and sits on the shaded canyon side, it is a pleasant pick when the weather is hot. It sees steady traffic, so expect company on weekends.

co_lone_eagle_peak.blurb: A remote granite spire of about 11,900 feet in the Indian Peaks, just west of the Continental Divide. It is a committed alpine objective: reaching its base takes a long hike from either side of the range, and many parties camp near the lakes below to split the effort. The big north-facing relief carries the best-known line, a long, moderate rock climb of eleven pitches with some loose gullies. Other lines on the east flank are harder, with several around 5.10 and one 5.11, and there is a fourth-class way to the summit that also serves as the descent. Expect exposure, quick storms and a long day.
